title: Secret Storage and Rotation
description: Learn how to store API keys, database passwords, and certificates safely. Explore environment variables, Azure Key Vault, rotation policies, and .NET integration patterns for secret management.

data.text: Secrets — API keys, database passwords, OAuth client secrets, and certificate private keys — are the keys to your kingdom. If an attacker obtains a secret, they can access databases, impersonate services, or exfiltrate user data. Secret storage and rotation are the practices that keep these keys safe throughout their lifecycle. The goal is simple: make secrets hard to steal, limit the damage if they are stolen, and replace them regularly.

Never hardcode secrets in source code. Never commit them to Git. The most basic option is environment variables, which keep secrets out of code and are supported by every deployment platform. For production, use a dedicated secrets manager like Azure Key Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or HashiCorp Vault. These services encrypt secrets at rest, audit access, and support fine-grained access control so that only specific services can read specific secrets.

terms.definition: A service that stores, manages, and rotates secrets such as API keys and passwords, with encryption and access auditing.
The practice of replacing a secret on a scheduled basis to limit the window of exposure if the secret is stolen.
An identity automatically managed by Azure that lets a service authenticate to Key Vault and other resources without storing any secret.
A security model that assumes no implicit trust and verifies every request, including those from inside the network.

data.content: Use a managed identity to authenticate to Key Vault and retrieve a secret at runtime.

data.title: Environment variables are not a vault
data.text: Environment variables are visible to any process running on the same machine, appear in crash dumps, and may be logged by deployment scripts. Use them for development convenience, but store production secrets in a proper secrets manager with encryption, audit logging, and access policies.

Rotation means replacing a secret on a regular schedule. When a secret is rotated, the old value remains valid during a transition window while dependent services are updated. Once all services use the new value, the old value is revoked. This limits the blast radius: if a secret is stolen, it is only useful until the next rotation. For high-value secrets like database passwords and signing keys, rotate every 30-90 days. For API keys shared with third parties, negotiate rotation windows that minimize downtime.

data.title: Rotation best practices
items: Store the secret in a versioned secrets manager that supports multiple active versions.
Deploy the application with the new secret value while keeping the old value valid.
Verify the application is working with the new secret.
Revoke the old secret and remove it from the application's configuration.
Log the rotation event and alert on any failures.

data.text: Rotation in .NET with Azure Key Vault

Azure Key Vault supports automatic rotation through Azure Key Vault secrets and Event Grid integration. You can configure a rotation policy that triggers a Lambda or Azure Function to generate a new secret value and update the Key Vault. The application reloads its configuration on the next request (or via a push refresh) and starts using the new value. For .NET, the Azure.Extensions.AspNetCore.Configuration.Secrets package automatically handles reload when secrets change.

data.title: Automatic configuration reload with Key Vault
data.content: The application reloads secrets from Key Vault when they change.

data.text: Client-side JavaScript must never contain secrets. Anything bundled into a JavaScript application is visible to anyone who opens the browser DevTools. API keys for third-party services should be called through a backend proxy, not directly from the browser. If a third-party service requires an API key in client-side code, that service is not designed for browser use — use their server-side SDK instead.

data.title: Backend proxy for third-party API
data.content: The React app calls your backend, which holds the secret and forwards the request.

items.text: Store all production secrets in a managed secrets vault.
items.hint: Azure Key Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or HashiCorp Vault.

items.text: Use managed identities instead of client secrets when running in the cloud.
items.hint: Managed identities eliminate the secret entirely.
Automate rotation with vault features or CI/CD pipelines.

items.text: Never put secrets in client-side JavaScript or mobile app bundles.
items.hint: All client-side code is fully visible to users.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Secrets must never appear in source code, client-side bundles, or environment variables in production.
Use a managed secrets vault with encryption, access policies, and audit logging.
Rotate secrets regularly to limit the window of exposure after theft.
Managed identities remove the need for secrets entirely in cloud environments.
data.takeaway: Secrets are like house keys: store them in a safe, change the locks regularly, and never leave copies under the mat.
